newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban's new allies take control of Afghan city.
newsitem.headline: Taleban's new allies take control of Afghan city.

text.p: Forces opposed to defeated Afghan warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum consolidated their grip on the northern capital of Mazar-i-Sharif on Sunday.

Ethnic Uzbek fighters loyal to General Abdul Malik, who launched an anti-Dostum mutiny on Monday, appeared to be in full control of the city, a day after they swept in from the west, brushing aside half-hearted resistance.
The rebels tore down a huge portrait of Dostum in the city when they arrived, replacing it with Malik.
They also put up portraits of Malik's brother, Rasul Pahlivan, a former Dostum commander assassinated last year.
White flags, emblem of the purist Taleban Islamic militia, fluttered from the rebels' vehicles, although the fighters all appeared to be northerners.
Mazar-i-Sharif was the last major Afghan city to hold out against the Taleban, who now control most of the country.
A Shi'ite Moslem militia was still resisting them in the central city of Bamiyan, while former government military commander Ahmed Shah Masood held part of the northeast.
The Taleban captured the northern provinces of Samangan and Kunduz on Sunday from Dostum's forces, the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) news service said.
General Majid Rouzi, a Malik supporter, appeared at Mazar's main Hazrat Ali mosque, where he made a speech telling the people of Mazar-i-Sharif to resume their normal lives.
"Everyone can come out," he said. "It's safe and if anyone does anything wrong to you, please inform us."
A Moslem cleric then took over the loudspeaker, saying people should congratulate themselves because the power of Dostum, a former communist general, had finally been broken.
Dostum is believed to have fled, possibly to neighbouring Uzbekistan, but there was no firm word on his whereabouts.
"Everyone trusts Malik, everyone likes him," the cleric said. "He agrees to work with Islamic law under (Taleban leader) Amir-ul-Momineen (leader of the faithful) Mullah Mohammad Omar."
Witnesses said Malik's fighters had looted the money changers' markets and some shops when they first arrived, but soldiers were later ordered to curb the pillage.

A truckload of fighters raided the U.N. guest house where several foreign journalists were staying on Saturday, taking a satellite television decoder, walkie-talkies and thermos flasks after hitting a local guard with a rifle butt.
Malik's security chief, Ghulam Rasul, toured the city centre. and told reporters: "There is no security problem and there is no looting. We have brought security."
Crowds of civilians, almost all men and boys, milled around in the streets, but shops remained shuttered, markets stalls were empty and there were no private cars in sight.
Malik forces were also in control of Dostum's base at Qala-i-Jhangi (fortress of war), a vast mud-walled fortress about 20 km (13 miles) southwest of Mazar-i-Sharif.
Abdul Ahad, a rebel commander told reporters outside the walls of the citadel that Dostum's forces fought for one hour before surrendering.

Ahad said his unit of ethnic Uzbek fighters fought alongside some Taleban to capture on Saturday Shibarghan, 130 km (81 miles) west of Mazar-i-Sharif, where Dostum had his military headquarters and main air base.
"Dostum was a cruel person and we were tired of fighting," he said. "The Afghan people are fed up with war."
Asked his opinion about the Taleban, Ahad said: "For constructing a widely supported government, we are ready to work with anyone who wants an independent Afghanistan."

He denied there had been fighting on the road between Shibarghan and Mazar-i-Sharif, but another rebel commander told reporters on Saturday that 30 of his fighters had died in the advance, and at least 100 Dostum troops had been killed.
At the village of Sherabat, about five km (three miles) from Mazar-i-Sharif, civilians were tearing down a mud-filled post where Dostum's troops had once manned a checkpoint.
"We are doing this on General Rouzi's orders," said one villager, Atta Mohammed. "The soldiers here used to make trouble for us. They would beat people. Now we have peace."
